DISCHARGE SUMMARY

Admission 16 November 2025, discharge 18 November 2025. Two nights, acute medical unit then diabetes ward.

Diagnosis: diabetic ketoacidosis precipitated by a pump infusion set occlusion during an intercurrent gastroenteritis.

On arrival: capillary ketones 5.2 mmol/L, venous pH 7.19, bicarbonate 11 mmol/L, capillary glucose 27.4 mmol/L, potassium 4.8 mmol/L. Alert and orientated throughout, no shock, no infection focus other than the gastrointestinal illness.

Management: fixed-rate intravenous insulin infusion and fluid replacement per the trust ketoacidosis protocol, with the pump suspended during treatment. Ketosis cleared at fourteen hours. Potassium replaced in the second and third litres. The pump was restarted with a new infusion set and a fresh site the following morning under supervision.

At discharge: eating and drinking normally, ketones negative, glucose 8.9 mmol/L, back on hybrid closed-loop with his usual settings.

Actions: sick-day rules reinforced with the diabetes specialist nurse, ketone meter and strips re-supplied, infusion set technique reviewed, technology clinic follow-up arranged.

Section 1.3 is a second narrow support: an eGFR of 60 to 89 with nothing else is not CKD, which does NOT support 'the patient has normal kidneys' or 'no monitoring is needed'.

NORTHFIELD RENAL NETWORK
STANDARD: CLASSIFICATION OF CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE AND MONITORING INTERVALS
Version 4.0, effective 18 March 2026.

1. Classification. Chronic kidney disease is classified by GFR category and albuminuria category together; a GFR category quoted without an albuminuria category is an incomplete classification.
1.1 GFR categories: G1 is an eGFR of 90 mL/min/1.73m2 or above with other evidence of kidney damage; G2 is 60 to 89 with other evidence of kidney damage; G3a is 45 to 59; G3b is an eGFR of 30 to 44 mL/min/1.73m2; G4 is 15 to 29; G5 is below 15 or on renal replacement therapy.
1.2 Albuminuria categories, by urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio on an early morning sample: A1 is below 3 mg/mmol; A2 is 3 to 30 mg/mmol; A3 is above 30 mg/mmol.
1.3 An eGFR of 60 to 89 with no albuminuria, no haematuria, no structural abnormality and no genetic diagnosis is not chronic kidney disease and should not be coded as such.

2. Chronicity. A single eGFR below 60 mL/min/1.73m2 does not establish chronic kidney disease. The abnormality must be present for at least three months. Where a reduced eGFR is new, repeat it within two weeks to exclude acute kidney injury, and again at three months to establish chronicity. A new result more than 25 per cent below the patient's own recent baseline should be treated as possible acute kidney injury and investigated on that footing while the repeat is awaited.

3. Monitoring intervals, in the absence of an intercurrent illness or a recent drug change.
3.1 G1 or G2 with A1: annually where a risk factor is present; not otherwise indicated.
3.2 G3a with A1: 12-monthly. G3a with A2: 6-monthly. G3a with A3: 3-monthly.
3.3 G3b with A1 or A2: 6-monthly. G3b with A3: 3-monthly.
3.4 G4: 3-monthly, with each measurement to include potassium, bicarbonate, calcium, phosphate, parathyroid hormone and haemoglobin.
3.5 G5 not on dialysis: 6-weekly, under nephrology supervision.
3.6 Each measurement means eGFR and urine albumin-to-creatinine ratio together.

4. Rate of decline. A decline of more than 5 mL/min/1.73m2 in one year, or more than 10 mL/min/1.73m2 in five years, is progressive chronic kidney disease and warrants a cause review whatever the current stage.

5. Referral to nephrology. Refer for a fall in eGFR of 25 per cent or more accompanied by a change of GFR category within 12 months; a sustained fall of 15 mL/min/1.73m2 or more within 12 months; an albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 70 mg/mmol or above unless known to be due to diabetes and already treated; an albumin-to-creatinine ratio of 30 mg/mmol or above with haematuria; G4 or G5 of any cause; suspected genetic kidney disease; or hypertension uncontrolled on four agents.

6. Out of scope. Acute kidney injury is staged separately by the rise in creatinine and by urine output, and is not covered by this standard. An eGFR reported during an acute illness must not be used to assign a chronic kidney disease stage.

MEADOWBANK DIABETES NETWORK
PROTOCOL: DIABETIC FOOT RISK STRATIFICATION AND REVIEW INTERVALS
Version 3.2, effective 12 November 2025.

1. The examination. Every adult with diabetes has a foot check at diagnosis and at least annually thereafter. The check records: skin condition and callus; deformity including claw toes, hallux valgus, Charcot deformity and prominent metatarsal heads; footwear adequacy; sensation using a 10 g monofilament at four sites on each foot, with loss of sensation at any one site counted as loss of protective sensation; dorsalis pedis and posterior tibial pulses by palpation, with ankle-brachial pressure index measured where either pulse is absent; and the presence of any ulcer, however small.

2. Risk categories.
2.1 Low risk: no loss of protective sensation, both pulses present, no deformity, no previous ulceration and no previous amputation. Callus alone does not raise the category. Review annually.
2.2 Moderate risk: any one of loss of protective sensation, peripheral arterial disease (an absent pulse or an ankle-brachial pressure index below 0.9), or deformity. Review three to six monthly.
2.3 High risk: previous ulceration; previous amputation; loss of protective sensation together with peripheral arterial disease; loss of protective sensation or peripheral arterial disease together with callus or deformity; or renal replacement therapy. Review one to two monthly.
2.4 Active diabetic foot problem: any ulceration, spreading infection, critical limb ischaemia, gangrene, or an unexplained hot, swollen or red foot. Refer to the multidisciplinary foot service within one working day. Do not wait for the next scheduled review.

3. Renal disease. Any person receiving haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis, and any person with a functioning kidney transplant, is classified as high risk irrespective of the examination findings, because the ulceration and amputation rates in this group are high even where sensation and pulses are intact. Reduced eGFR alone, without renal replacement therapy, does not by itself change the category, but an eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73m2 should prompt review of the category at each contact.

4. Charcot neuroarthropathy. Suspect it in any person with loss of protective sensation and a hot, swollen foot, with or without pain and with or without a history of injury. Refer the same day, offload the foot immediately, and do not wait for a radiograph, which is normal in the early stage.

5. What a normal examination does and does not establish. A foot examination that finds no ulceration records the absence of active ulceration on the day of the examination. It does not by itself place the person in the low risk category, and it does not reduce a category previously assigned on the basis of loss of protective sensation, peripheral arterial disease, previous ulceration or previous amputation. Those four factors are treated as permanent for the purposes of this stratification: neuropathy and previous ulceration do not resolve, and a person once assigned to the high risk category remains in it.

6. Education at every review. Daily inspection including between the toes and with a mirror for the sole; never walk barefoot; check footwear for foreign objects before putting shoes on; test bath water with the hand or an elbow; and who to telephone the same day if a break in the skin appears.

GADOVEXAN 0.5 mmol/mL solution for injection
PRESCRIBING INFORMATION (ABRIDGED) - Caldermere Pharma Limited
Label version 2.1, text revised 09 February 2026.

4.1 Therapeutic indications. Macrocyclic gadolinium-based contrast agent for magnetic resonance imaging of the central nervous system, the abdomen and the musculoskeletal system, and for magnetic resonance angiography, in adults and children.

4.2 Posology and method of administration. The standard adult dose is 0.1 mmol/kg body weight given as a single intravenous injection. Use the lowest dose consistent with a diagnostic examination. Do not exceed a single dose of 0.1 mmol/kg and do not repeat within seven days where the eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73m2.

4.3 Contraindications. Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any excipient.

4.4 Special warnings and precautions for use.
4.4.1 Renal function. Obtain an eGFR within three months before an elective examination and within seven days for inpatients and patients with acute illness. The renal concern with gadolinium-based agents is nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, not acute kidney injury.
4.4.2 Nephrogenic systemic fibrosis. Cases have been reported in patients with an eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73m2, in patients on any form of dialysis, in acute kidney injury, and in the perioperative liver transplant period. GADOVEXAN is a macrocyclic agent and the reported risk with macrocyclic agents is very low, but the precautions in section 4.2 apply and the examination should be justified against a non-contrast alternative.
4.4.3 Dialysis. In a patient already established on haemodialysis, arrange a session as soon as possible after administration. Do not initiate dialysis solely to remove GADOVEXAN in a patient not already receiving it; there is no evidence that doing so prevents nephrogenic systemic fibrosis.
4.4.4 Acute kidney injury. Contrast-associated acute kidney injury has not been demonstrated at approved doses of gadolinium-based agents, and intravenous volume expansion is not required on renal grounds before or after GADOVEXAN. Correct clinically apparent volume depletion for the usual reasons.
4.4.5 Metformin. Metformin does not require withholding before or after administration of GADOVEXAN at any level of renal function.
4.4.6 Gadolinium retention. Traces of gadolinium are retained in brain, bone and skin after repeated administration. No clinical consequence has been established; nevertheless keep a cumulative record where repeated contrast-enhanced imaging is planned.

4.8 Undesirable effects. Common: headache, nausea, injection site coolness. Uncommon: rash, dizziness. Rare: hypersensitivity reactions.

10. Scope of this document. This prescribing information applies to GADOVEXAN and to gadolinium-based contrast agents of the same class. It does not apply to iodinated contrast media used for computed tomography and angiography. The renal precautions for iodinated media differ in kind: they address acute kidney injury rather than nephrogenic systemic fibrosis, and they include a volume expansion regimen, a post-procedure creatinine check and a conditional metformin withholding requirement, none of which appear in this document and none of which may be inferred from it.

MEADOWBANK DIABETES NETWORK
STANDARD: INTERPRETATION OF HbA1c, AND THE CONDITIONS IN WHICH IT CANNOT BE INTERPRETED
Version 2.3, effective 07 July 2025.

1. Reporting. HbA1c is reported in mmol/mol (IFCC). Percentages (DCCT) may be quoted alongside but the mmol/mol value is the one recorded. 48 mmol/mol corresponds to 6.5 per cent and 53 mmol/mol to 7.0 per cent.

2. Targets. 48 mmol/mol for a person managed on lifestyle measures or on a drug not associated with hypoglycaemia; 53 mmol/mol for a person on a sulfonylurea or insulin; 58 to 64 mmol/mol where the person is frail, has limited life expectancy, has hypoglycaemia unawareness, or where tighter control has already caused harm. Relaxing a target is a documented decision, not a drift.

3. What the number measures. HbA1c reflects mean glycaemia over the preceding 8 to 12 weeks, weighted towards the most recent four weeks. It says nothing about variability and nothing about hypoglycaemia; a person with frequent hypoglycaemia and frequent hyperglycaemia can return a value at target. Do not repeat within three months, because the preceding result is still substantially within the window being measured.

4. Conditions in which HbA1c cannot be interpreted. The assay measures glycation of haemoglobin over the lifespan of the red cell, so anything that shortens, lengthens or replaces that lifespan invalidates the result.
4.1 Falsely low: haemolysis of any cause, recent major blood loss, splenomegaly and hypersplenism, transfusion within the preceding three months, erythropoiesis-stimulating agents, iron or vitamin B12 replacement started within the preceding three months, pregnancy in the second and third trimesters.
4.2 Falsely high: untreated iron deficiency anaemia, untreated vitamin B12 or folate deficiency, splenectomy, alcohol excess.
4.3 Unpredictable or assay-dependent: haemoglobin variants including HbS, HbC and beta-thalassaemia trait; carbamylation of haemoglobin in advanced uraemia. HbA1c is unreliable in CKD stage 4 and stage 5, in patients on haemodialysis or peritoneal dialysis, and in patients on an erythropoiesis-stimulating agent at any stage of CKD; in these groups the result typically underestimates mean glycaemia and must not be used to relax or intensify treatment on its own.
4.4 Where HbA1c cannot be interpreted, use a structured capillary glucose profile, continuous glucose monitoring metrics, or fructosamine, and record which measure the treatment decision was based on.

5. Chronic kidney disease stages 3a and 3b. At an eGFR of 30 to 59 mL/min/1.73m2, with a stable haemoglobin and no erythropoiesis-stimulating agent, HbA1c remains a valid index of mean glycaemia and may be used and targeted in the usual way. Check the full blood count alongside the HbA1c so that a falling haemoglobin is not mistaken for improving control.

6. Diagnosis. A single HbA1c of 48 mmol/mol or above in an asymptomatic person must be confirmed by a second sample before diabetes is diagnosed. HbA1c must not be used for diagnosis in children, in pregnancy, in suspected type 1 diabetes, in symptoms of less than two months' duration, or in any of the conditions listed in section 4.

MEADOWBANK DIABETES NETWORK
PROTOCOL: INITIATION AND TITRATION OF BASAL INSULIN IN TYPE 2 DIABETES
Version 4.1, effective 22 October 2025. For use in primary care and community diabetes services.

1. Scope and exclusions. Adults with type 2 diabetes starting a once-daily basal insulin analogue or once-daily isophane insulin as an addition to oral therapy. This protocol does not cover type 1 diabetes, insulin pump therapy, twice-daily mixed insulin regimens, or insulin prescribed during an inpatient admission.

2. Before starting. Confirm the HbA1c is above the individualised target on maximum tolerated oral therapy. Record weight, eGFR, current glucose-lowering drugs, driving status and occupation. Issue a meter, strips and a written hypoglycaemia plan. Continue metformin. Stop any sulfonylurea or reduce it by half at the point of insulin initiation.

3. Starting dose. Begin with a starting dose of 10 units once daily at bedtime, or 0.2 units per kilogram of body weight, whichever is the smaller. In a patient over 75 years of age, or with an eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73m2, or weighing under 60 kg, begin with 6 units.

4. Fasting glucose target. The default target for the pre-breakfast capillary glucose is 6 to 8 mmol/L. Use a target of 7 to 9 mmol/L where the patient is over 75, frail, lives alone, has hypoglycaemia unawareness, or has an eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73m2.

5. Titration. The patient titrates against the mean of the last three pre-breakfast readings.
5.1 Mean above the upper limit of target: increase the dose by 2 units every three days until the mean is within target.
5.2 Mean within target: no change.
5.3 Mean below the lower limit of target: reduce the dose by 2 units.
5.4 After any capillary glucose below 3.0 mmol/L, or any symptomatic nocturnal hypoglycaemia at any reading, reduce the dose by 4 units or by 10 per cent, whichever is the larger, and hold further titration for one week.
5.5 Do not titrate on the basis of a single reading.

6. Renal function and insulin requirement. Insulin is cleared in part by the kidney and the requirement falls as renal function declines; a patient whose eGFR is falling may need less insulin than the same patient needed a year earlier. Where the eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73m2, reduce the titration increment to 1 unit every three days, apply the 7 to 9 mmol/L target from section 4, and review the total daily dose at every clinic contact. A fall in insulin requirement in a patient whose diet has not changed should prompt a check of renal function rather than an assumption of improved control.

7. Review. Telephone or message review at two weeks, then four-weekly until the fasting target is met for two consecutive weeks. Recheck HbA1c three months after initiation.

8. When to seek specialist advice. Total daily dose above 0.5 units per kilogram without the fasting target being met; any severe hypoglycaemia requiring third-party help; fasting readings at target but HbA1c still above target after three months, which indicates postprandial rather than basal failure and is not corrected by further basal titration.

IOHEXALAN 350 mg iodine/mL solution for injection
PRESCRIBING INFORMATION (ABRIDGED) - Caldermere Pharma Limited
Label version 3.0, text revised 14 January 2026.

4.1 Therapeutic indications. Intravascular iodinated contrast medium for computed tomography, digital subtraction angiography and urography in adults and children over one year.

4.2 Posology and method of administration. Dose is determined by the examination and by body weight; use the lowest dose that will answer the clinical question. In adults with an eGFR below 45 mL/min/1.73m2 the total iodine load should be kept below 350 mg iodine per kilogram of body weight where the examination allows. Do not repeat an intravascular contrast examination within 48 hours in a patient with an eGFR below 45 mL/min/1.73m2 unless the second examination cannot be deferred.

4.3 Contraindications. Hypersensitivity to the active substance or to any excipient. Manifest thyrotoxicosis. Intrathecal administration; IOHEXALAN is not formulated for intrathecal use and inadvertent intrathecal administration may cause convulsions.

4.4 Special warnings and precautions for use.
4.4.1 Renal function. Obtain an eGFR within three months before an elective examination, and within seven days for any inpatient, any patient with acute illness, and any patient with known chronic kidney disease. Contrast-associated acute kidney injury is uncommon after intravenous administration and no specific renal prophylaxis is required for intravenous administration where the eGFR is 30 mL/min/1.73m2 or above. Where the eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73m2, where administration is intra-arterial with first-pass renal exposure, or where acute kidney injury is present or suspected, discuss the examination with the radiologist and give intravenous volume expansion with sodium chloride 0.9 per cent at 1 mL/kg/hour for 6 hours before and 6 hours after administration, adjusted for cardiac failure.
4.4.2 Monitoring after administration. Where the eGFR is below 45 mL/min/1.73m2, recheck serum creatinine 48 to 72 hours after administration.
4.4.3 Metformin. Withhold metformin from the time of administration and for the following 48 hours where the eGFR is below 30 mL/min/1.73m2, where administration is intra-arterial with first-pass renal exposure, or where acute kidney injury is present or suspected; renal function must be rechecked and shown to be stable before metformin is restarted. Withholding metformin is not required for intravenous administration where the eGFR is 30 mL/min/1.73m2 or above. The concern is accumulation of metformin if contrast precipitates a fall in renal clearance, not an interaction between metformin and the contrast medium itself.
4.4.4 Other nephrotoxic agents. Consider withholding non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drugs and aminoglycosides around the examination. Diuretics need not be stopped routinely but volume depletion should be corrected before administration.
4.4.5 Thyroid. Iodinated contrast may precipitate hyperthyroidism in patients with autonomous nodules and may interfere with radioiodine uptake for up to two months.

4.8 Undesirable effects. Common: warmth or flushing on injection, nausea, altered taste. Uncommon: urticaria, extravasation injury. Rare: severe hypersensitivity reactions, contrast-associated acute kidney injury.

10. Scope of this document. This prescribing information relates to iodinated contrast media. Gadolinium-based contrast agents are the subject of separate prescribing information and different renal precautions apply to them.

NORTHFIELD REGIONAL MEDICINES OPTIMISATION NETWORK
PRESCRIBING GUIDELINE: METFORMIN IN CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE
Version 2.0, effective 18 April 2024. Ratified by the Network Prescribing Committee.

1. Scope. Immediate-release and modified-release metformin hydrochloride in adults with type 2 diabetes and reduced or declining renal function, in primary care and general medical clinics. Fixed-dose combination products containing metformin are in scope; the metformin component determines the ceiling dose.

2. Renal review threshold. Review the metformin dose where the eGFR falls below 45 mL/min/1.73m2. The review should record the indication, the current dose, the trend in renal function over the preceding twelve months, and whether an alternative agent is appropriate. An isolated result below 45 in a patient with an intercurrent illness should be repeated before the dose is changed.

3. Dose ceiling by renal function.
3.1 eGFR 45 mL/min/1.73m2 and above: standard prescribing applies, to a maximum of 2000 mg daily in divided doses.
3.2 eGFR 30 to 44 mL/min/1.73m2: the maximum total daily dose is 1000 mg, given as 500 mg twice daily. Where a patient is already established on a higher dose, reduce to the ceiling at the next review rather than stopping abruptly.
3.3 Do not initiate metformin de novo in a patient whose eGFR is already below 45 mL/min/1.73m2.

4. Discontinuation. Discontinue metformin where the eGFR falls below 30 mL/min/1.73m2. Below this level metformin is contraindicated because renal clearance of the drug is insufficient to prevent accumulation, and accumulation is the mechanism of metformin-associated lactic acidosis.

5. Monitoring interval. Check renal function at least annually where the eGFR is 60 mL/min/1.73m2 or above, six-monthly at 45 to 59, and three-monthly at 30 to 44. Check sooner after any acute illness, after starting a diuretic, an ACE inhibitor, an angiotensin receptor blocker or a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, and before and after iodinated contrast administration.

6. Intercurrent illness. Withhold metformin during any illness that causes dehydration, vomiting, diarrhoea lasting more than twelve hours, or sepsis, and during any admission with hypotension or hypoxia. Restart once the patient has been eating and drinking normally for 48 hours and renal function has been rechecked.

7. Vitamin B12. Check serum vitamin B12 every two to three years in patients on long-term metformin, and sooner where there is anaemia or peripheral neuropathy.

Amendment 2.0a, 05 June 2026: typographical correction to the units printed in section 3.2. No threshold, dose or interval in this document has been changed by the amendment.

PRESCRIBING GUIDELINE: METFORMIN IN CHRONIC KIDNEY DISEASE
Version 3.0, effective 11 May 2026. Ratified by the Network Prescribing Committee.
This version supersedes version 2.0 of April 2024, which should be withdrawn from local use.

1. Scope. Unchanged from the previous version: immediate-release and modified-release metformin hydrochloride in adults with type 2 diabetes and reduced or declining renal function. Fixed-dose combination products containing metformin are in scope.

2. Renal review threshold. Review the metformin dose where the eGFR falls below 60 mL/min/1.73m2. The review should record the indication, the current dose, the trend in renal function over the preceding twelve months, and whether an alternative agent is appropriate.

3. Dose ceiling by renal function.
3.1 eGFR 60 mL/min/1.73m2 and above: standard prescribing applies, to a maximum of 2000 mg daily in divided doses.
3.2 eGFR 45 to 59 mL/min/1.73m2: the maximum total daily dose is 1000 mg, given as 500 mg twice daily.
3.3 Do not initiate metformin de novo in a patient whose eGFR is already below 60 mL/min/1.73m2.

4. Discontinuation. Discontinue metformin where the eGFR falls below 45 mL/min/1.73m2.
4.1 Transition. A patient already established on metformin with an eGFR between 30 and 44 mL/min/1.73m2 should have the drug stopped at a planned review within three months, with an alternative glucose-lowering agent considered at the same appointment. Abrupt discontinuation without a plan for glycaemic control is not required and is not intended by this section.
4.2 A patient with an eGFR below 30 mL/min/1.73m2 should stop metformin immediately.

5. Monitoring interval. Check renal function at least annually where the eGFR is 60 mL/min/1.73m2 or above, six-monthly at 45 to 59, and three-monthly below 45 while any transition plan is in progress. Check sooner after any acute illness, after starting a diuretic, an ACE inhibitor, an angiotensin receptor blocker or a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, and before and after iodinated contrast administration.

6. Intercurrent illness. Withhold metformin during any illness that causes dehydration, vomiting, diarrhoea lasting more than twelve hours, or sepsis, and during any admission with hypotension or hypoxia. Restart once the patient has been eating and drinking normally for 48 hours and renal function has been rechecked.

7. Vitamin B12. Check serum vitamin B12 every two to three years in patients on long-term metformin, and sooner where there is anaemia or peripheral neuropathy.

8. Record of change from version 2.0. Following a network review of metformin-associated lactic acidosis incident reports, the discontinuation threshold has been raised from an eGFR of 30 to an eGFR of 45 mL/min/1.73m2, the review threshold from 45 to 60, and the 1000 mg ceiling has been moved up one CKD stage accordingly. No other section has changed in substance.

MONITORING STANDARD: RENAL FUNCTION AND POTASSIUM AFTER STARTING OR INCREASING AN ACE INHIBITOR OR ANGIOTENSIN RECEPTOR BLOCKER
Version 1.3, effective 05 September 2023.

1. Baseline. Measure serum creatinine, eGFR and serum potassium within two weeks before starting an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin receptor blocker, or before any dose increase. Record the baseline values in the notes; the acceptable-change thresholds in section 3 are meaningless without them.

2. Repeat testing. Recheck renal function and serum potassium one to two weeks after initiation and after every dose increase. Where the patient is also taking a diuretic, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist or a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, recheck at one week.

3. Acceptable change. A rise in serum creatinine of up to 30 per cent from baseline, or a fall in eGFR of up to 25 per cent, is an expected haemodynamic consequence of blocking the renin-angiotensin system and is not a reason to stop the drug, provided the value is stable when repeated and the patient is clinically well. Recheck again at four weeks and then at the interval set for the underlying indication.

4. Change beyond the acceptable range. Where the creatinine has risen by more than 30 per cent, or the eGFR has fallen by more than 25 per cent:
4.1 Look for and correct a reversible cause: hypovolaemia, intercurrent diarrhoea or vomiting, a recently started diuretic or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, or urinary obstruction.
4.2 If no reversible cause is found, halve the dose or stop the drug and recheck within one to two weeks.
4.3 Consider renovascular disease where the rise is abrupt, large, or occurs in a patient with widespread arterial disease, and refer for imaging.

5. Potassium. Stop the ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker where the serum potassium exceeds 6.0 mmol/L, and treat the hyperkalaemia on its merits. Where the potassium is 5.5 to 6.0 mmol/L, recheck within one week, review dietary potassium, and review every other drug that raises potassium before attributing the result to the renin-angiotensin blocker alone.

6. Combination. Do not prescribe an ACE inhibitor and an angiotensin receptor blocker together.

7. Sick-day advice. Advise the patient to withhold the drug during any illness causing dehydration and to seek advice about restarting.

a rise in serum creatinine of up to 30 per cent from baseline
a fall in eGFR of up to 25 per cent
where the serum potassium exceeds 6.0 mmol/L

NORTHFIELD REGIONAL MEDICINES OPTIMISATION NETWORK
MONITORING STANDARD: RENAL FUNCTION AND POTASSIUM AFTER STARTING OR INCREASING AN ACE INHIBITOR OR ANGIOTENSIN RECEPTOR BLOCKER
Version 3.0, effective 16 February 2026. This standard supersedes version 1.3 of September 2023 and the interim version 2.0.

1. Baseline. Measure serum creatinine, eGFR and serum potassium within two weeks before starting an ACE inhibitor or an angiotensin receptor blocker, or before any dose increase. A drug started without a recorded baseline cannot be monitored against this standard and the baseline should be obtained before the first dose.

2. Repeat testing. Recheck renal function and serum potassium 7 to 10 days after initiation and after every dose increase, and again at four weeks. Where the patient is also taking a diuretic, a mineralocorticoid receptor antagonist or a non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, or has an eGFR below 45 mL/min/1.73m2, recheck at 5 to 7 days.

3. Acceptable change. A rise in serum creatinine of up to 20 per cent from baseline, or a fall in eGFR of up to 15 per cent, is an expected haemodynamic consequence of blocking the renin-angiotensin system and is not a reason to stop the drug, provided the value is stable when repeated and the patient is clinically well.

4. Change beyond the acceptable range. Where the creatinine has risen by more than 20 per cent, or the eGFR has fallen by more than 15 per cent:
4.1 Look for and correct a reversible cause: hypovolaemia, intercurrent diarrhoea or vomiting, a recently started diuretic or non-steroidal anti-inflammatory drug, or urinary obstruction.
4.2 If no reversible cause is found, halve the dose and recheck within 7 days. Stop the drug if the second result has not settled within the acceptable range.
4.3 Consider renovascular disease where the rise is abrupt, large, or occurs in a patient with widespread arterial disease, and refer for imaging.

5. Potassium. Stop the ACE inhibitor or angiotensin receptor blocker where the serum potassium is 5.5 mmol/L or above, having first excluded a haemolysed or delayed sample by immediate repeat. Where the potassium is 5.0 to 5.4 mmol/L, continue at the same dose, recheck within one week, review dietary potassium and review every other drug that raises potassium.

6. Combination. Do not prescribe an ACE inhibitor and an angiotensin receptor blocker together.

7. Sick-day advice. Give written advice to withhold the drug during any illness causing dehydration, vomiting or diarrhoea, and to restart 48 hours after normal oral intake resumes.

8. Record of change from version 1.3. The repeat testing interval has moved from one to two weeks to 7 to 10 days; the acceptable rise in serum creatinine has been reduced from 30 to 20 per cent; the acceptable fall in eGFR has been reduced from 25 to 15 per cent; and the potassium discontinuation threshold has been reduced from above 6.0 mmol/L to 5.5 mmol/L or above. Sections 1, 4.1, 4.3 and 6 are unchanged.
key_facts: a rise in serum creatinine of up to 20 per cent from baseline
a fall in eGFR of up to 15 per cent
where the serum potassium is 5.5 mmol/L or above

PRESCRIBING GUIDELINE: SGLT2 INHIBITORS - RENAL USE, KETOACIDOSIS RISK AND SICK-DAY RULES
Version 2.2, effective 03 September 2025.

1. Scope. Dapagliflozin, empagliflozin and canagliflozin prescribed for type 2 diabetes, for chronic kidney disease, or for heart failure, in adults. Combination products containing an SGLT2 inhibitor are in scope.

2. Initiation by renal function.
2.1 Do not initiate an SGLT2 inhibitor where the eGFR is below 20 mL/min/1.73m2.
2.2 Between an eGFR of 20 and 44 mL/min/1.73m2 an SGLT2 inhibitor may be initiated for a renal or cardiovascular indication, but should not be initiated for glycaemic control alone.
2.3 At an eGFR of 45 mL/min/1.73m2 and above any licensed indication applies.

3. Expected early change in renal function. A fall in eGFR of up to 10 per cent, or a rise in serum creatinine of up to 15 per cent, within the first four weeks of starting is an expected haemodynamic effect. It is not an indication to stop and should not be reported as acute kidney injury. Recheck at four weeks; the eGFR should stabilise or recover thereafter.

4. Continuation as renal function declines. An SGLT2 inhibitor already established for a renal or cardiovascular indication may be continued as the eGFR falls, and need not be stopped on renal grounds alone until the initiation of dialysis or the receipt of a kidney transplant. Continuation is conditional on renal function being checked at least six-monthly and on the sick-day provisions in section 6 having been given to the patient in writing. Glucose-lowering efficacy is a separate question from organ protection: glucose-lowering efficacy falls progressively below an eGFR of 45 mL/min/1.73m2 and is minimal below 30, so a patient continued at these levels will usually need a different agent added if the HbA1c is above target.

5. Ketoacidosis, including euglycaemic ketoacidosis. SGLT2 inhibitors can precipitate diabetic ketoacidosis at glucose concentrations that would ordinarily be reassuring: ketoacidosis can occur with a blood glucose below 11 mmol/L, and the diagnosis has been missed for this reason.
5.1 Measure capillary or blood ketones in any patient taking an SGLT2 inhibitor who is unwell, nauseated, vomiting, breathless or abdominally tender, whatever the blood glucose.
5.2 Blood ketones 0.6 to 1.5 mmol/L: withhold the SGLT2 inhibitor, ensure carbohydrate and fluid intake, and recheck within two hours.
5.3 Blood ketones above 1.5 mmol/L, or any ketones with vomiting or breathlessness: withhold the drug and arrange same-day assessment for ketoacidosis.
5.4 Do not restart the SGLT2 inhibitor after an episode of ketoacidosis without specialist diabetes advice.

6. Sick-day rules. Withhold the SGLT2 inhibitor during any acute illness with reduced oral intake, vomiting, diarrhoea, fever with sweating, or suspected sepsis, and during any admission for acute illness. Restart only when the patient has been eating and drinking normally for 24 hours and is no longer ketotic.

7. Surgery and fasting. Withhold the SGLT2 inhibitor for three days before elective surgery, that is on the day of surgery and the three preceding days where a bowel preparation or a prolonged fast is planned, and do not restart until oral intake is re-established. Prolonged fasting with the drug on board is a recognised trigger for euglycaemic ketoacidosis.

8. Volume status. Review the dose of loop diuretic at initiation. Genital mycotic infection is common and is not by itself a reason to stop; recurrent infection or any suspicion of perineal pain out of proportion to findings should prompt urgent assessment.

9. Scope exclusion. The ketone-testing provisions in section 5 and the pre-operative withholding period in section 7 are specific to SGLT2 inhibitors and are not transferable to other glucose-lowering classes.
key_facts: Do not initiate an SGLT2 inhibitor where the eGFR is below 20 mL/min/1.73m2
ketoacidosis can occur with a blood glucose below 11 mmol/L
need not be stopped on renal grounds alone
Withhold the SGLT2 inhibitor for three days before elective surgery
glucose-lowering efficacy falls progressively below an eGFR of 45

NORTHFIELD MEDICINES SAFETY RULE ENGINE - DETERMINISTIC RULE OUTPUT
Rule SD-GLP1-02: withholding of GLP-1 receptor agonists during acute intercurrent illness.
Engine build 2026.2, rule revision 4. Reference evaluation run 12 June 2026 against the published worked input set; this is a catalogue entry, not an evaluation against a patient record.

1. Rule statement. IF the prescribed drug belongs to the GLP-1 receptor agonist class AND at least one of (vomiting for 12 hours or more; diarrhoea for 12 hours or more; oral intake reduced for 24 hours or more; documented acute kidney injury of any stage) THEN output = WITHHOLD, and restart when oral intake has been normal for 24 hours. Otherwise output = CONTINUE.

2. Inputs: drug class = GLP-1 receptor agonist (worked input set uses dulaglutide 1.5 mg once weekly); vomiting duration = 18 hours; diarrhoea duration = 0 hours; duration of reduced oral intake = 24 hours; acute kidney injury flag = false; most recent eGFR = 38 mL/min/1.73m2; capillary ketone measurement = not an input to this rule.

3. Evaluation. Class test satisfied. Two of the four symptom conditions satisfied (vomiting 18 hours, which is at or above the 12-hour bound; reduced oral intake 24 hours, which is at or above the 24-hour bound). Output: WITHHOLD.

4. Reproducibility. The rule is a conjunction of a class test and a disjunction of four bounded conditions. It contains no probabilistic component, no free-text interpretation and no dependence on evaluation date. The same six inputs return WITHHOLD on any engine in the 2026 series.

5. What this rule does not evaluate. The eGFR is carried as context only and does not enter the rule: GLP-1 receptor agonists have no eGFR-based withholding threshold in this catalogue, and a low eGFR alone will not fire this rule. The rule does not evaluate ketones, does not generate any pre-operative instruction, and does not consider glycaemic control.

6. Scope. Rule SD-GLP1-02 evaluates GLP-1 receptor agonists only. SGLT2 inhibitors are evaluated by rule SD-SGLT2-01, which carries a capillary ketone trigger and a three-day pre-operative withholding period that rule SD-GLP1-02 does not contain. Metformin is evaluated by rule SD-MET-03 and insulin by rule SD-INS-05. The output of this rule must not be read across to SGLT2 inhibitors, metformin or insulin; a WITHHOLD from this rule is a statement about the GLP-1 receptor agonist and about nothing else the patient is taking.

restart when oral intake has been normal for 24 hours

TRUST ANTICOAGULATION GUIDELINE - WARFARIN IN NON-VALVULAR ATRIAL FIBRILLATION
Version 3.1, effective 01 November 2025.

1. Target range. Patients with non-valvular atrial fibrillation should be maintained at a target INR range of 2.0 to 3.0, with 2.5 as the midpoint.

2. Results within range. No dose change is required for a result within range in a patient with stable recent history. Recheck at the interval set by the clinic protocol.

3. Results above range. For an INR above 4.5 without bleeding, omit warfarin and recheck within 48 hours. For an INR between 3.0 and 4.5 without bleeding, reduce the weekly dose by 10-20% and recheck within two weeks.

4. Renal impairment. Warfarin does not require dose adjustment on the basis of renal function alone. Declining renal function may nonetheless alter bleeding risk and should prompt review of the overall anticoagulation strategy rather than a change of warfarin dose per se.
